description: A binary passes user-controlled input directly as the format argument to printf() instead of using a fixed format string with the input as a data argument, e.g. printf(user_input) instead of printf("%s", user_input).
explanation: printf's format string controls how many arguments it reads off the stack (and, for %n, lets it WRITE to an address it reads off the stack). When the attacker controls the format string itself, they control both: %x/%p specifiers let them read arbitrary stack values (leaking saved addresses, canaries, pointers), and %n lets them write an attacker-chosen value to an attacker-chosen address, which is enough to overwrite a return address, a GOT entry, or any other useful target without needing a separate buffer overflow at all.
solve_steps: Confirm the vulnerability: pass a format specifier like %x or %p and see if it reflects stack data instead of being treated as literal text
Send a sequence of %p (or %x with explicit positional args like %7$p) to walk the stack and find the offset to your own input
Use %s at that offset to leak a pointer into libc or the binary (defeats ASLR the same way a ret2libc leak does)
Compute target addresses (e.g. a GOT entry to overwrite) from the leaked base
Build a %n-based write primitive (often via pwntools' fmtstr_payload) to overwrite the target with a chosen value
Trigger the overwritten code path (e.g. call the GOT-hijacked function) to get control
notes: Format string bugs are often faster to exploit than a stack overflow once the offset is found -- check for one before assuming you need ROP.
